{{Short description|Representation of the symmetry group of spacetime in special relativity}}
{{Good article}}{{Use American English|date = March 2019}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs2}}
[[File:Einstein en Lorentz.jpg|220px|thumb|right|[[Hendrik Antoon Lorentz]] (right) after whom the [[Lorentz group]] is named and [[Albert Einstein]] whose [[special theory of relativity]] is the main source of application. Photo taken by [[Paul Ehrenfest]] 1921.]]

The [[Lorentz group]] is a [[Lie group]] of symmetries of the [[spacetime]] of [[special relativity]].  This group can be realized as a collection of [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]], [[linear transformation]]s, or [[unitary operator]]s on some [[Hilbert space]]; it has a variety of [[Representations of Lie groups|representations]].<ref group=nb>The way in which one represents the spacetime symmetries may take many shapes depending on the theory at hand. While not being the present topic, some details will be provided in footnotes labeled "nb", and in the section [[#Applications|applications]].</ref>  This group is significant because special relativity together with [[quantum mechanics]] are the two physical theories that are most thoroughly established,<ref group=nb>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|p=1}} ''"If it turned out that a system could not be described by a quantum field theory, it would be a sensation; if it turned out it did not obey the rules of quantum mechanics and relativity, it would be a cataclysm."''</ref> and the conjunction of these two theories is the study of the infinite-dimensional unitary representations of the Lorentz group.  These have both historical importance in mainstream physics, as well as connections to more speculative present-day theories.

{{TOC limit|2}}

The development of the representation theory has historically followed the development of the more general theory of representation theory of [[semisimple group]]s, largely due to [[Élie Cartan]] and [[Hermann Weyl]], but the Lorentz group has also received special attention due to its importance in physics. Notable contributors are physicist [[E. P. Wigner]] and mathematician [[Valentine Bargmann]] with their [[Bargmann–Wigner equations|Bargmann–Wigner program]],<ref>{{harvnb|Bargmann|Wigner|1948}}</ref> one conclusion of which is, roughly, ''a classification of all unitary representations of the inhomogeneous Lorentz group amounts to a classification of all possible relativistic wave equations''.<ref>{{harvnb|Bekaert|Boulanger|2006}}</ref> The classification of the irreducible infinite-dimensional representations of the Lorentz group was established by [[Paul Dirac]]'s doctoral student in theoretical physics, [[Harish-Chandra]], later turned mathematician,<ref group=nb>In 1945, Harish-Chandra came to see Dirac in Cambridge. Harish-Chandra became convinced that theoretical physics was not the field he should be in. He had found an error in a proof by Dirac in his work on the Lorentz group. Dirac said, "I am not interested in proofs but only interested in what nature does." Harish-Chandra later wrote, "This remark confirmed my growing conviction that I did not have the mysterious sixth sense which one needs in order to succeed in physics, and I soon decided to move over to mathematics." Dirac did, however, suggest the topic of Harish-Chandra's thesis, the classification of the irreducible infinite-dimensional representations of the Lorentz group.
See {{harvnb|Dalitz|Peierls|1986}}</ref> in 1947. Closely related work was published independently by Bargmann and [[Israel Gelfand]] together with [[Mark Naimark]] in the same year.

The full theory of the finite-dimensional representations of the [[Lie algebra]] of the Lorentz group is deduced using the general framework of the representation theory of [[semisimple Lie algebra]]s. The finite-dimensional representations of the connected component <math>\text{SO}(3; 1)^+</math> of the full Lorentz group {{math|O(3; 1)}} are obtained by employing the [[Lie correspondence]] and the [[matrix exponential]]. The full finite-dimensional representation theory of the [[universal covering group]] (and also the [[spin group]], a double cover) <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> of <math>\text{SO}(3; 1)^+</math> is obtained, and explicitly given in terms of action on a function space in [[#Representations of SL(2, C) and sl(2, C)|representations of <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> and <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex)</math>]]. The representatives of [[T-symmetry|time reversal]] and [[Parity (physics)|space inversion]] are given in [[#Space inversion and time reversal|space inversion and time reversal]], completing the finite-dimensional theory for the full Lorentz group. The general [[#Properties of the (m, n) representations|properties of the (''m'', ''n'') representations]] are outlined. [[#Action on function spaces|Action on function spaces]] is considered, with the action on [[#Spherical harmonics|spherical harmonics]] and the [[#The Riemann P-functions|Riemann P-function]]s appearing as examples. The infinite-dimensional case of irreducible unitary representations is realized for the <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> [[#Principal series for SL(2, C)|principal series]] and the [[complementary series]]. Finally, the [[#Plancherel theorem for SL(2, C)|Plancherel formula]] for <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> is given, and representations of {{math|SO(3, 1)}} are [[#Classification of representations of SO(3, 1)|classified]] and realized for Lie algebras.

== Finite-dimensional representations ==
Representation theory of groups in general, and Lie groups in particular, is a very rich subject. The Lorentz group has some properties that makes it "agreeable" and others that make it "not very agreeable" within the context of representation theory; the group is [[simple (abstract algebra)|simple]] and thus [[Semisimple Lie algebra|semisimple]], but is not [[Connected set|connected]], and none of its components are [[simply connected space|simply connected]]. Furthermore, the Lorentz group is not [[compact space|compact]].<ref>These facts can be found in most introductory mathematics and physics texts. See e.g. {{harvtxt|Rossmann|2002}}, {{harvtxt|Hall|2015}} and {{harvtxt|Tung|1985}}.</ref>

For finite-dimensional representations, the presence of semisimplicity means that the Lorentz group can be dealt with the same way as other semisimple groups using a well-developed theory. In addition, all representations are built from the [[Irreducible representation|irreducible]] ones, since the Lie algebra possesses the ''complete reducibility property''.<ref group=nb>{{harvtxt|Hall|2015|loc=Section 4.4.}}
{{Paragraph break}}
One says that a group has the ''complete reducibility property'' if every representation decomposes as a direct sum of irreducible representations.</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Hall|2015|loc=Theorem 4.34 and following discussion.}}</ref> But, the non-compactness of the Lorentz group, in combination with lack of simple connectedness, cannot be dealt with in all the aspects as in the simple framework that applies to simply connected, compact groups. Non-compactness implies, for a connected simple Lie group, that no nontrivial finite-dimensional [[Unitary representation|unitary]] representations exist.<ref name="Wigner 1939">{{harvnb|Wigner|1939}}</ref> Lack of simple connectedness gives rise to [[spin representation]]s of the group.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015|loc=Appendix D2.}}</ref> The non-connectedness means that, for representations of the full Lorentz group, [[T-symmetry|time reversal]] and [[Parity (physics)|reversal of spatial orientation]] have to be dealt with separately.<ref name="greiner-reinhardt-1996">{{harvnb|Greiner|Reinhardt|1996}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Section 2.6 and Chapter 5.}}</ref>

=== History ===
The development of the finite-dimensional representation theory of the Lorentz group mostly follows that of representation theory in general. Lie theory originated with [[Sophus Lie]] in 1873.<ref name="Coleman 1989 30">{{harvnb|Coleman|1989|p=30.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Lie|1888}}, 1890, 1893. Primary source.</ref> By 1888 the [[list of simple lie groups|classification of simple Lie algebras]] was essentially completed by [[Wilhelm Killing]].<ref>{{harvnb|Coleman|1989|p=34.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Killing|1888}} Primary source.</ref> In 1913 the [[Theorem on highest weights|theorem of highest weight]] for representations of simple Lie algebras, the path that will be followed here, was completed by [[Élie Cartan]].<ref name="Rossmann 2002 loc=Historical tidbits scattered across the text">{{harvnb|Rossmann|2002|loc=Historical tidbits scattered across the text.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Cartan|1913}} Primary source.</ref> [[Richard Brauer]] was during the period of 1935–38 largely responsible for the development of the [[Weyl-Brauer matrices]] describing how spin representations of the Lorentz Lie algebra can be embedded in [[Clifford algebra]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Green|1998|loc=p=76.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Brauer|Weyl|1935}} Primary source.</ref> The Lorentz group has also historically received special attention in representation theory due to its exceptional importance in physics (see [[#infinite-dimensional unitary representations#history|History of infinite-dimensional unitary representations]] below). Mathematicians [[Hermann Weyl]]<ref name="Rossmann 2002 loc=Historical tidbits scattered across the text"/><ref>{{harvnb|Tung|1985|loc=Introduction.}}</ref><ref name="Coleman 1989 30"/><ref>{{harvnb|Weyl|1931}} Primary source.</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Weyl|1953}} Primary source.</ref> and [[Harish-Chandra]]<ref>{{harvnb|Langlands|1985|pp=203–205}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Harish-Chandra|1947}} Primary source.</ref> and physicists [[Eugene Wigner]]<ref>{{harvnb|Tung|1985|loc=Introduction}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Wigner|1939}} Primary source.</ref> and [[Valentine Bargmann]]<ref>{{harvnb|Klauder|1999}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Bargmann|1947}} Primary source.</ref><ref>Bargmann was also a [[mathematician]]. He worked as [[Albert Einstein]]s assistant at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in Princeton ({{harvtxt|Klauder|1999}}).</ref> made substantial contributions both to general representation theory and in particular to the Lorentz group.<ref>{{harvnb|Bargmann|Wigner|1948}} Primary source.</ref> Physicist [[Paul Dirac]] was perhaps the first to manifestly knit everything together in a practical application of major lasting importance with the [[Dirac equation]] in 1928.<ref>{{harvnb|Dalitz|Peierls|1986}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Dirac|1928}} Primary source.</ref><ref group=nb>Dirac suggested the topic of {{harvtxt|Wigner|1939}} as early as 1928 (as acknowledged in Wigner's paper). He also published one of the first papers on explicit infinite-dimensional unitary representations in {{harvtxt|Dirac|1945}} ({{harvnb|Langlands|1985}}), and suggested the topic for Harish-Chandra's thesis classifying irreducible infinite-dimensional representations ({{harvnb|Dalitz|Peierls|1986}}).</ref>

===Lie algebra===
[[File:Wilhelm Karl Joseph Killing.jpeg|upright|thumb|[[Wilhelm Killing]], Independent discoverer of [[Lie algebra]]s. The simple Lie algebras were first classified by him in 1888.]]
The irreducible representations of the Lie algebra of the Lorentz group can be derived by factoring that Lie algebra into a direct product of two subalgebras. Each subalgebra is isomorphic to <math>\mathfrak{su}(2)</math>, and the irreducible representations of <math>\mathfrak{su}(2)</math> are labeled by nonnegative half-integers. Consequently, the irreducible representations of the Lorentz group's Lie algebra are labeled by ordered pairs <math>(m,n)</math> of nonnegative half-integers.{{sfn|Tung|1985|p=187}}

This section addresses the irreducible complex linear representations of the [[complexification]] <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1)_\Complex</math> of the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1)</math> of the Lorentz group.  A convenient basis for <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1)</math> is given by the three [[#Explicit formulas|generators]] {{math|''J''<sub>''i''</sub>}} of [[rotation]]s and the three generators {{math|''K''<sub>''i''</sub>}} of [[Lorentz boost|boost]]s. They are explicitly given in [[#Conventions and Lie algebra bases|conventions and Lie algebra bases]].

The Lie algebra is [[Complexification (Lie group)|complexified]], and the basis is changed to the components of its two ideals<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Equations 5.6.7–8.}}</ref>
<math display="block">\mathbf{A} = \frac{\mathbf{J} + i \mathbf{K}}{2},\quad \mathbf{B} = \frac{\mathbf{J} - i \mathbf{K}}{2}.</math>

The components of {{math|1='''A''' = (''A''<sub>1</sub>, ''A''<sub>2</sub>, ''A''<sub>3</sub>)}} and {{math|1='''B''' = (''B''<sub>1</sub>, ''B''<sub>2</sub>, ''B''<sub>3</sub>)}} separately satisfy the [[commutation relation]]s of the Lie algebra [[su(2)|<math>\mathfrak{su}(2)</math>]] and, moreover, they commute with each other,<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Equations 5.6.9–11.}}</ref>

<math display="block">\left[A_i, A_j\right] = i\varepsilon_{ijk} A_k,\quad \left[B_i, B_j\right] = i\varepsilon_{ijk} B_k,\quad \left[A_i, B_j\right] = 0,</math>

where {{math|''i'', ''j'', ''k''}} are indices which each take values {{math|1, 2, 3}}, and {{math|''ε<sub>ijk</sub>''}} is the three-dimensional [[Levi-Civita symbol]]. Let <math>\mathbf{A}_\Complex</math> and <math>\mathbf{B}_\Complex</math> denote the complex [[linear span]] of {{math|'''A'''}} and {{math|'''B'''}} respectively.

One has the isomorphisms<ref name="Hall 2003">{{harvnb|Hall|2003|loc=Chapter 6.}}</ref><ref group=nb>{{harvnb|Knapp|2001}} The rather mysterious looking third isomorphism is proved in chapter 2, paragraph 4.</ref>
{{NumBlk|| <math display="block">\begin{align}
      \mathfrak{so}(3; 1) \hookrightarrow
        \mathfrak{so}(3; 1)_\Complex &\cong
        \mathbf{A}_\Complex \oplus \mathbf{B}_\Complex
      \cong \mathfrak{su}(2)_\Complex  \oplus  \mathfrak{su}(2)_\Complex \\[5pt]
      &\cong \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex) \oplus  \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex) \\[5pt]
      &\cong \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex) \oplus i\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex) =
        \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)_\Complex \hookleftarrow \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex),
    \end{align}</math>
| {{EquationRef|A1|A1}}
}}
where <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)</math> is the complexification of <math>\mathfrak{su}(2) \cong \mathbf{A} \cong \mathbf{B}.</math>

The utility of these isomorphisms comes from the fact that all irreducible [[Representation theory of SU(2)|representations of <math>\mathfrak{su}(2)</math>]], and hence all irreducible complex linear representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex),</math> are known. The irreducible complex linear representation of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)</math> is isomorphic to one of the [[highest weight representation]]s. These are explicitly given in [[#Complex linear representations|complex linear representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex).</math>]]<ref name="Hall 2003"/>

====Unitarian trick====
[[File:Hermann Weyl ETH-Bib Portr 00890.jpg|upright|thumb|right|[[Hermann Weyl]], inventor of the [[unitarian trick]]. There are several concepts and formulas in representation theory named after Weyl, e.g. the [[Weyl group]] and the [[Weyl character formula]]. ]]

The Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex) \oplus \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)</math> is the Lie algebra of <math>\text{SL}(2, \Complex) \times \text{SL}(2, \Complex).</math> It contains the compact subgroup {{math|SU(2) × SU(2)}} with Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{su}(2).</math> The latter is a compact real form of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex) \oplus \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex).</math> Thus from the first statement of the unitarian trick, representations of {{math|SU(2) × SU(2)}} are in one-to-one correspondence with holomorphic representations of <math>\text{SL}(2, \Complex) \times \text{SL}(2, \Complex).</math>

By compactness, the [[Peter–Weyl theorem]] applies to {{math|SU(2) × SU(2)}},<ref name="ReferenceC">{{harvnb|Knapp|2001}}</ref> and hence orthonormality of [[irreducible character]]s may be appealed to. The irreducible unitary representations of {{math|SU(2) × SU(2)}} are precisely the [[tensor product]]s of irreducible unitary representations of {{math|SU(2)}}.<ref>This is an application of {{harvnb|Rossmann|2002|loc=Section 6.3, Proposition 10.}}</ref>

By appeal to simple connectedness, the second statement of the unitarian trick is applied. The objects in the following list are in one-to-one correspondence:
* Holomorphic representations of <math>\text{SL}(2, \Complex) \times \text{SL}(2, \Complex)</math>
* Smooth representations of {{math|SU(2) × SU(2)}}
* Real linear representations of <math>\mathfrak{su}(2) \oplus \mathfrak{su}(2)</math>
* Complex linear representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex) \oplus \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)</math>

Tensor products of representations appear at the Lie algebra level as either of<ref group="nb">Tensor products of representations, {{math|''π<sub>g</sub>'' ⊗ ''π<sub>h</sub>''}} of <math>\mathfrak{g} \oplus \mathfrak{h}</math> can, when both factors come from the same Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{h} = \mathfrak{g},</math> either be thought of as a representation of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> or <math>\mathfrak{g} \oplus \mathfrak{g}</math>.</ref>
{{NumBlk|| <math display="block">\begin{align}
        \pi_1\otimes\pi_2(X) &= \pi_1(X) \otimes \mathrm{Id}_V + \mathrm{Id}_U \otimes \pi_2(X) && X \in \mathfrak{g} \\
     \pi_1\otimes\pi_2(X, Y) &= \pi_1(X) \otimes \mathrm{Id}_V + \mathrm{Id}_U \otimes \pi_2(Y) && (X, Y) \in \mathfrak{g} \oplus \mathfrak{g}
   \end{align}</math>
 | {{EquationRef|A0|A0}}
}}
where {{math|Id}} is the identity operator. Here, the latter interpretation, which follows from {{EquationNote|G6|(G6)}}, is intended. The highest weight representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)</math> are indexed by {{mvar|μ}} for {{math|1=''μ'' = 0, 1/2, 1, ...}}. (The highest weights are actually {{math|1=2''μ'' = 0, 1, 2, ...}}, but the notation here is adapted to that of <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1).</math>) The tensor products of two such complex linear factors then form the irreducible complex linear representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex) \oplus \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex).</math>

Finally, the <math>\R</math>-linear representations of the [[real form (Lie theory)|real forms]] of the far left, <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1)</math>, and the far right, <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex),</math><ref group=nb>When complexifying a ''complex'' Lie algebra, it should be thought of as a ''real'' Lie algebra of real dimension twice its complex dimension. Likewise, a real form may actually also be complex as is the case here.</ref> in {{EquationNote|A1|(A1)}} are obtained from the <math>\Complex</math>-linear representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex) \oplus \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)</math> characterized in the previous paragraph.

==== (''μ'', ''ν'')-representations of sl(2, C) ====
The complex linear representations of the complexification of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex), \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)_\Complex,</math> obtained via isomorphisms in {{EquationNote|A1|(A1)}}, stand in one-to-one correspondence with the real linear representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex).</math><ref name="Knapp 2001 32">{{harvnb|Knapp|2001|p=32.}}</ref> The set of all ''real linear'' irreducible representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)</math> are thus indexed by a pair {{math|(''μ'', ''ν'')}}. The complex linear ones, corresponding precisely to the complexification of the real linear <math>\mathfrak{su}(2)</math> representations, are of the form {{math|(''μ'', 0)}}, while the conjugate linear ones are the {{math|(0, ''ν'')}}.<ref name="Knapp 2001 32"/> All others are real linear only. The linearity properties follow from the canonical injection, the far right in {{EquationNote|A1|(A1)}}, of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)</math> into its complexification. Representations on the form {{math|(''ν'', ''ν'')}} or {{math|(''μ'', ''ν'') ⊕ (''ν'', ''μ'')}} are given by ''real'' matrices (the latter are not irreducible). Explicitly, the real linear {{math|(''μ'', ''ν'')}}-representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)</math> are
<math display="block">\varphi_{\mu, \nu}(X) =
  \left(\varphi_\mu \otimes \overline{\varphi_\nu}\right)(X) =
  \varphi_\mu(X) \otimes \operatorname{Id}_{\nu+1} + \operatorname{Id}_{\mu+1} \otimes \overline{\varphi_\nu(X)},\qquad X \in \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)
</math>
where <math display="inline">\varphi_\mu, \mu = 0, \tfrac{1}{2}, 1, \tfrac{3}{2}, \ldots</math> are the complex linear irreducible representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)</math> and <math>\overline{\varphi_\nu}, \nu = 0, \tfrac{1}{2}, 1, \tfrac{3}{2}, \ldots</math> their complex conjugate representations. (The labeling is usually in the mathematics literature {{math|0, 1, 2, ...}}, but half-integers are chosen here to conform with the labeling for the <math>\mathfrak{so}(3, 1)</math> Lie algebra.) Here the tensor product is interpreted in the former sense of {{EquationNote|A0|(A0)}}. These representations are [[#Concrete realization|concretely realized]] below.

==== (''m'', ''n'')-representations of so(3; 1) ====
Via the displayed isomorphisms in {{EquationNote|A1|(A1)}} and knowledge of the complex linear irreducible representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex) \oplus \mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)</math> upon solving for {{math|'''J'''}} and {{math|'''K'''}}, all irreducible representations of <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1)_\Complex,</math> and, by restriction, those of <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1)</math> are obtained. The representations of <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1)</math> obtained this way are real linear (and not complex or conjugate linear) because the algebra is not closed upon conjugation, but they are still irreducible.<ref name="Hall 2003"/> Since <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1)</math> is [[semisimple Lie algebra|semisimple]],<ref name="Hall 2003"/> all its representations can be built up as [[direct sum]]s of the irreducible ones.

Thus the finite dimensional irreducible representations of the Lorentz algebra are classified by an ordered pair of half-integers {{math|1=''m'' = ''μ''}} and {{math|1=''n'' = ''ν''}}, conventionally written as one of
<math display="block">(m, n) \equiv \pi_{(m,n)} : \mathfrak{so}(3;1) \to \mathfrak{gl}(V),</math>
where {{mvar|V}} is a finite-dimensional vector space. These are, up to a [[Matrix similarity|similarity transformation]], uniquely given by<ref group=nb>Combine {{harvtxt|Weinberg|2002|loc=Equations 5.6.7–8, 5.6.14–15}} with {{harvtxt|Hall|2015|loc=Proposition 4.18}} about Lie algebra representations of group tensor product representations.</ref>
{{NumBlk||
<math display="block">\pi_{(m,n)}(J_i) = J^{(m)}_i \otimes 1_{(2n+1)}+1_{(2m+1)} \otimes J^{(n)}_i </math>
<math display="block">\pi_{(m,n)}(K_i) = -i \left(J^{(m)}_i \otimes 1_{(2n+1)} - 1_{(2m+1)} \otimes J^{(n)}_i\right), </math>
| {{EquationRef|A2|A2}} }}
where {{math|1<sub>''n''</sub>}} is the {{mvar|n}}-dimensional [[Identity matrix|unit matrix]] and
<math display="block">\mathbf{J}^{(n)} = \left(J^{(n)}_1, J^{(n)}_2, J^{(n)}_3\right)</math>
are the {{math|(2''n'' + 1)}}-dimensional irreducible [[Representation theory of SU(2)|representations of <math>\mathfrak{so}(3) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2)</math>]] also termed [[Rotation group SO(3)#A note on Lie algebras|spin matrices]] or ''angular momentum matrices''. These are explicitly given as<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Equations 5.6.16–17.}}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \left(J_1^{(j)}\right)_{a'a} &= \frac{1}{2} \left(\sqrt{(j - a)(j + a + 1)}\delta_{a',a + 1} + \sqrt{(j + a)(j - a + 1)}\delta_{a',a - 1}\right) \\
  \left(J_2^{(j)}\right)_{a'a} &= \frac{1}{2i}\left(\sqrt{(j - a)(j + a + 1)}\delta_{a',a + 1} - \sqrt{(j + a)(j - a + 1)}\delta_{a',a - 1}\right) \\
  \left(J_3^{(j)}\right)_{a'a} &= a\delta_{a',a}
\end{align}</math>
where {{math|''δ''}} denotes the [[Kronecker delta]]. In components, with {{math|−''m'' ≤ ''a'', ''a′'' ≤ ''m''}}, {{math|−''n'' ≤ ''b'', ''b′'' ≤ ''n''}}, the representations are given by<ref name="Weinberg 2002 Chapter 2">{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Section 5.6.}} The equations follow from equations 5.6.7–8 and 5.6.14–15.</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \left(\pi_{(m,n)}\left(J_i\right)\right)_{a'b', ab} &= \delta_{b'b} \left(J_i^{(m)}\right)_{a'a} + \delta_{a'a} \left(J_i^{(n)}\right)_{b'b}\\
  \left(\pi_{(m,n)}\left(K_i\right)\right)_{a'b', ab} &= -i \left( \delta_{b'b} \left(J_i^{(m)}\right)_{a'a} - \delta_{a'a} \left(J_i^{(n)}\right)_{b'b}\right)
\end{align}</math>

Representations of this Lie algebra are used in physics, since various physical quantities of interest are functions, or collections of functions, defined on spacetime that transform together under a representation of an appropriate dimension.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Chapter 5}}</ref>

* The {{math|(0, 0)}} representation is the one-dimensional [[trivial representation]] and is carried by relativistic [[scalar field]] theories.<ref>{{harvnb|Tung|1985|p=203}}</ref>
* Fermionic [[supersymmetry]] generators transform under one of the {{math|(0, {{sfrac|1|2}})}} or {{math|({{sfrac|1|2}}, 0)}}  representations (Weyl spinors).<ref name="Weinberg 2000 loc=Section 25.2">{{harvnb|Weinberg|2000|loc=Section 25.2.}}</ref>
* The [[four-momentum]] of a [[particle]] (either massless or [[invariant mass|massive]]) transforms under the {{math|({{sfrac|1|2}}, {{sfrac|1|2}})}} representation, a [[four-vector]].<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Sections 2.5 and 5.1}}</ref>
* A physical example of a (1,1) traceless [[symmetric bilinear form|symmetric]] [[tensor field]] is the traceless<ref group=nb>The "traceless" property can be expressed as {{math|1=''S''<sub>''αβ''</sub>[[metric tensor (general relativity)|''g'']]<sup>''αβ''</sup> = 0}}, or {{math|1=''S''<sub>''α''</sub><sup>''α''</sup> = 0}}, or {{math|1=''S''<sup>''αβ''</sup>''g''<sub>''αβ''</sub> = 0}} depending on the presentation of the field: covariant, mixed, and contravariant respectively.</ref> part of the [[energy–momentum tensor]] {{mvar|T<sup>μν</sup>}}.<ref name="Tung 1985">{{harvnb|Tung|1985}}</ref><ref group=nb>This doesn't necessarily come symmetric directly from the Lagrangian by using [[Noether's theorem]], but it can be symmetrized as the [[Belinfante–Rosenfeld stress–energy tensor]].</ref>

Since complex conjugation exchanges {{math|(''m'', ''n'')}} and {{math|(''n'', ''m'')}}, the [[direct sum of representations]] {{math|(''m'', ''n'')}} and {{math|(''n'', ''m'')}} admits real matrix representatives and therefore has particular relevance to physics.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2003|p=219}}</ref><ref name="weinberg-2002-5.7">{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Section 5.7}}</ref>

* {{math|({{sfrac|1|2}}, 0) ⊕ (0, {{sfrac|1|2}})}} is the [[Dirac spinor]] representation. See also [[#Weyl spinors|Weyl spinors]] below.
* {{math|(1, {{sfrac|1|2}}) ⊕ ({{sfrac|1|2}}, 1)}} is the [[Rarita–Schwinger equation|Rarita–Schwinger]] field representation.
* {{math|({{sfrac|3|2}}, 0) ⊕ (0, {{sfrac|3|2}})}} would be the symmetry of the hypothesized [[gravitino]].<ref group=nb>This is provided parity is a symmetry. Else there would be two flavors, {{math|({{sfrac|3|2}}, 0)}} and {{math|(0, {{sfrac|3|2}})}} in analogy with [[neutrino]]s.</ref> It can be obtained from the {{math|(1, {{sfrac|1|2}}) ⊕ ({{sfrac|1|2}}, 1)}} representation.
* {{math|(1, 0) ⊕ (0, 1)}} is the representation of a [[P-symmetry|parity]]-invariant [[2-form]] field (a.k.a. [[curvature form]]). The [[electromagnetic field tensor]] transforms under this representation.

=== Group ===
The approach in this section is based on theorems that, in turn, are based on the fundamental [[Lie correspondence]].<ref>{{harvnb|Lie|1888}}</ref> The Lie correspondence is in essence a dictionary between connected Lie groups and Lie algebras.<ref>{{harvnb|Rossmann|2002|loc=Section 2.5.}}</ref> The link between them is the [[exponential map (Lie theory)|exponential mapping]] from the Lie algebra to the Lie group, denoted <math>\exp : \mathfrak{g} \to G.</math>

If <math>\pi : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{gl}(V)</math> for some vector space {{mvar|V}} is a representation, a representation {{math|Π}} of the connected component of {{mvar|G}} is defined by
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\begin{align}
\Pi(g = e^{iX}) &\equiv e^{i\pi(X)}, && X \in \mathfrak g, \quad g = e^{iX} \in \mathrm{im}(\exp),\\
\Pi(g = g_1g_2\cdots g_n) &\equiv \Pi(g_1)\Pi(g_2)\cdots \Pi(g_n), && g \notin \mathrm{im}(\exp), \quad g_1 , g_2, \ldots, g_n \in \mathrm{im}(\exp).
\end{align}</math>|{{EquationRef|G2|G2}}}}

This definition applies whether the resulting representation is projective or not.

==== Surjectiveness of exponential map for SO(3, 1) ====
From a practical point of view, it is important whether the first formula in {{EquationNote|G2|(G2)}} can be used for all elements of the ''group''. It holds for all <math>X \in \mathfrak{g}</math>, however, in the general case, e.g. for <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math>, not all {{math|''g'' ∈ ''G''}} are in the image of {{math|exp}}.

But <math>\exp : \mathfrak{so}(3;1) \to \text{SO}(3;1)^+</math> ''is'' surjective. One way to show this is to make use of the isomorphism <math>\text{SO}(3; 1)^+ \cong \text{PGL}(2,\Complex),</math> the latter being the [[Möbius group]]. It is a quotient of <math>\text{GL}(n,\Complex)</math> (see the linked article). The quotient map is denoted with <math>p : \text{GL}(n,\Complex) \to \text{PGL}(2,\Complex).</math> The map <math>\exp : \mathfrak{gl}(n, \Complex) \to \text{GL}(n, \Complex)</math> is onto.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015|loc=Theorem 2.10.}}</ref> Apply {{EquationNote|Lie|(Lie)}} with {{mvar|π}} being the differential of {{mvar|p}} at the identity. Then

<math display="block">\forall X \in \mathfrak{gl}(n, \Complex): \quad  p ( \exp (iX)) =\exp ( i \pi (X)).</math>

Since the left hand side is surjective (both {{math|exp}} and {{mvar|p}} are), the right hand side is surjective and hence <math>\exp : \mathfrak{pgl}(2, \Complex) \to \text{PGL}(2, \Complex)</math> is surjective.<ref>{{harvnb|Bourbaki|1998|p=424.}}</ref> Finally, recycle the argument once more, but now with the known isomorphism between {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} and <math>\text{PGL}(2, \Complex)</math> to find that {{math|exp}} is onto for the connected component of the Lorentz group.

==== Fundamental group ====
The Lorentz group is ''doubly connected'', i. e.  {{math|''π''<sub>1</sub>(SO(3; 1))}} is a group with two equivalence classes of loops as its elements.
{{math proof | proof =
To exhibit the [[fundamental group]] of {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}}, the topology of its [[#The covering group SL(2, C)|covering group <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math>]] is considered. By the [[polar decomposition theorem]], any matrix <math>\lambda \in \text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> may be ''uniquely'' expressed as<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Section 2.7 p.88.}}</ref>

<math display="block">\lambda = ue^h,</math>

where {{mvar|u}} is [[Unitary matrix|unitary]] with [[determinant]] one, hence in {{math|SU(2)}}, and {{mvar|h}} is [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian]] with [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]] zero. The [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]] and [[determinant]] conditions imply:<ref name="Weinberg 2002 loc=Section 2.7">{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Section 2.7.}}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
h &= \begin{pmatrix}c&a-ib\\a+ib&-c\end{pmatrix} && (a,b,c) \in \R^3 \\[4pt]
u &= \begin{pmatrix}d+ie&f+ig\\-f+ig&d-ie\end{pmatrix} && (d,e,f,g) \in \R^4 \text{ subject to } d^2 + e^2 + f^2 + g^2 = 1.
\end{align}</math>

The manifestly continuous one-to-one map is a [[homeomorphism]] with continuous inverse given by (the locus of {{mvar|u}} is identified with <math>\mathbb{S}^3 \subset \R^4</math>)

<math display="block">\begin{cases} \R^3 \times \mathbb{S}^3\to \text{SL}(2, \Complex) \\ (r,s) \mapsto u(s) e^{h(r)} \end{cases}</math>

explicitly exhibiting that <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> is simply connected. But <math>\text{SO}(3; 1)\cong \text{SL}(2,\Complex)/\{\pm I\},</math> where <math>\{\pm I\}</math> is the center of <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math>. Identifying {{mvar|λ}} and {{math|−''λ''}} amounts to identifying {{mvar|u}} with {{math|−''u''}}, which in turn amounts to identifying [[antipodal point]]s on <math>\mathbb{S}^3.</math> Thus topologically,<ref name="Weinberg 2002 loc=Section 2.7"/>
<math display="block">\text{SO}(3; 1) \cong \R^3 \times ( \mathbb{S}^3/\Z_2),</math>

where last factor is not simply connected: Geometrically, it is seen (for visualization purposes, <math>\mathbb{S}^3</math> may be replaced by <math>\mathbb{S}^2</math>) that a path from {{mvar|u}} to {{math|−''u''}} in <math>SU(2) \cong \mathbb{S}^3</math> ''is'' a loop in <math>\mathbb{S}^3/\Z_2</math> since {{mvar|u}} and {{math|−''u''}} are antipodal points, and that it is not contractible to a point. But a path from {{mvar|u}} to {{math|−''u''}}, thence to {{mvar|u}} again, a loop in <math>\mathbb{S}^3</math> and a ''double loop'' (considering {{math|1=''p''(''ue<sup>h</sup>'') = ''p''(−''ue<sup>h</sup>'')}}, where <math>p : \text{SL}(2,\Complex)\to \text{SO}(3; 1)</math> is the covering map) in <math>\mathbb{S}^3/\Z_2</math> that ''is'' contractible to a point (continuously move away from {{math|−''u''}} "upstairs" in <math>\mathbb{S}^3</math> and shrink the path there to the point {{mvar|u}}).<ref name="Weinberg 2002 loc=Section 2.7"/> Thus {{math|''π''<sub>1</sub>(SO(3; 1))}} is a group with two equivalence classes of loops as its elements, or put more simply, {{math|SO(3; 1)}} is ''doubly connected''.
}}

==== Projective representations ====
Since {{math|π<sub>1</sub>(SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>)}} has two elements, some representations of the Lie algebra will yield [[projective representation]]s.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015|loc=Appendix C.3.}}</ref><ref group=nb>The terminology differs between mathematics and physics. In the linked article term projective representation has a slightly different meaning than in physics, where a projective representation is thought of as a local section (a local inverse) of the [[covering map]] from the covering group onto the group being covered, composed with a proper representation of the covering group. Since this can be done (locally) continuously in two ways in the case at hand as explained below, the terminology of a double-valued or two-valued representation is natural.</ref> Once it is known whether a representation is projective, formula {{EquationNote|G2|(G2)}} applies to all group elements and all representations, including the projective ones — with the understanding that the representative of a group element will depend on which element in the Lie algebra (the {{mvar|X}} in {{EquationNote|G2|(G2)}}) is used to represent the group element in the standard representation.

For the Lorentz group, the {{math|(''m'', ''n'')}}-representation is projective when {{math|''m'' + ''n''}} is a half-integer. See {{section link||Spinors}}.

For a projective representation {{math|Π}} of {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}}, it holds that<ref name="Weinberg 2002 loc=Section 2.7"/>
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">
  \left[ \Pi(\Lambda_1)\Pi(\Lambda_2)\Pi^{-1}(\Lambda_1\Lambda_2) \right]^2 = 1 \Rightarrow
         \Pi(\Lambda_1\Lambda_2) = \pm\Pi(\Lambda_1)\Pi(\Lambda_2),\quad \Lambda_1, \Lambda_2 \in \mathrm{SO}(3; 1),</math>
 |{{EquationRef|G5|G5}}
}}
since any loop in {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} traversed twice, due to the double connectedness, is [[contractible]] to a point, so that its homotopy class is that of a constant map. It follows that {{math|Π}} is a double-valued function. It is not possible to consistently choose a sign to obtain a continuous representation of all of {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}}, but this is possible ''locally'' around any point.<ref name="Wigner 1939"/>

=== Covering group SL(2, C) ===
Consider <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex)</math> as a ''real'' Lie algebra with basis

<math display="block">\left(\frac{1}{2}\sigma_1, \frac{1}{2}\sigma_2, \frac{1}{2}\sigma_3, \frac{i}{2}\sigma_1, \frac{i}{2}\sigma_2, \frac{i}{2}\sigma_3\right)\equiv(j_1, j_2, j_3, k_1, k_2, k_3),</math>

where the sigmas are the [[Pauli matrices]]. From the relations
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">[\sigma_i, \sigma_j] = 2i\epsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k</math>|{{EquationRef|J1|J1}}}}
is obtained
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">[j_i, j_j] = i\epsilon_{ijk}j_k, \quad [j_i, k_j] = i\epsilon_{ijk}k_k, \quad [k_i, k_j] = -i\epsilon_{ijk}j_k,</math>|{{EquationRef|J2|J2}}}}
which are exactly on the form of the {{math|3}}-dimensional version of the commutation relations for <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1)</math> (see [[#Conventions and Lie algebra bases|conventions and Lie algebra bases]] below). Thus, the map {{math|''J''<sub>''i''</sub>  ↔  ''j''<sub>''i''</sub>}}, {{math|''K''<sub>''i''</sub> ↔ ''k''<sub>''i''</sub>}}, extended by linearity is an isomorphism. Since <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> is simply connected, it is the [[universal covering group]] of {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}}.

{{Hidden begin| titlestyle = color:green;background:lightgrey;|title=More on covering groups in general and the <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> covering of the Lorentz group in particular}}

==== A geometric view ====
[[File:Wigner.jpg|upright|thumb|[[Eugene Wigner|E.P. Wigner]] investigated the Lorentz group in depth and is known for the [[Bargmann-Wigner equations]]. The realization of the covering group given here is from his 1939 paper.]]

Let {{math|''p<sub>g</sub>''(''t''), 0 ≤ ''t'' ≤ 1}} be a path from {{math|1 ∈ SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} to {{math|''g'' ∈ SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}}, denote its homotopy class by {{math|[''p<sub>g</sub>'']}} and let {{mvar|π<sub>g</sub>}} be the set of all such homotopy classes. Define the set
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">G = \{(g,[p_g]): g\in \mathrm{SO}(3; 1)^+,[p_g]\in \pi_g\} </math>|{{EquationRef|C1|C1}}}}
and endow it with the multiplication operation
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">(g_1,[p_1])(g_2,[p_2]) = (g_1g_2,[p_{12}]),</math>|{{EquationRef|C2|C2}}}}
where <math>p_{12}</math> is the [[Fundamental group#Definition|path multiplication]] of <math>p_1</math> and <math>p_2</math>:

<math display="block">p_{12} (t) = (p_1 * p_2)(t) = \begin{cases} p_1(2t) & 0 \leqslant t \leqslant \tfrac{1}{2} \\ p_2(2t-1) & \tfrac{1}{2} \leqslant t \leqslant 1 \end{cases}</math>

With this multiplication, {{mvar|G}} becomes a [[group (mathematics)|group]] isomorphic to <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex),</math><ref>{{harvnb|Wigner|1939|p=27.}}</ref> the universal covering group of {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}}. Since each {{mvar|π<sub>g</sub>}} has two elements, by the above construction, there is a [[covering map|2:1 covering map]] {{math|''p'' : ''G'' → SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}}. According to [[covering group]] theory, the Lie algebras <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1), \mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex)</math> and <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> of {{mvar|G}} are all isomorphic. The covering map {{math|''p'' : ''G'' → SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} is simply given by {{math|1=''p''(''g'', [''p<sub>g</sub>'']) = ''g''}}.

==== An algebraic view ====
For an algebraic view of the universal covering group, let <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> act on the set of all Hermitian {{gaps|2|×|2}} matrices <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> by the operation<ref name="Weinberg 2002 loc=Section 2.7"/>
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\begin{cases}
\mathbf{P}(A): \mathfrak{h} \to \mathfrak{h} \\
X \mapsto A^\dagger XA
\end{cases} \qquad A \in \mathrm{SL}(2,\Complex)</math>|{{EquationRef|C3|C3}}}}

The action on <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> is linear. An element of <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> may be written in the form
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">X = \begin{pmatrix} \xi_4 + \xi_3&\xi_1 + i\xi_2\\ \xi_1 - i\xi_2&\xi_4 - \xi_3\\ \end{pmatrix} \qquad \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_4 \in \R.</math>|{{EquationRef|C4|C4}}}}

The map {{math|'''P'''}} is a group homomorphism into <math>\text{GL}(\mathfrak{h}) \subset \text{End}(\mathfrak{h}).</math> Thus <math>\mathbf{P} : \text{SL}(2,\Complex) \to \text{GL}(\mathfrak{h})</math> is a 4-dimensional representation of <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math>. Its kernel must in particular take the identity matrix to itself, {{math|1=''A''<sup>†</sup>''IA'' = ''A''<sup>†</sup>''A'' = ''I''}} and therefore {{math|1=''A''<sup>†</sup> = ''A''<sup>−1</sup>}}. Thus {{math|1=''AX'' = ''XA''}} for {{mvar|A}} in the kernel so, by [[Schur's lemma]],<ref group=nb>In particular, {{math|''A''}} commutes with the [[Pauli matrices]], hence with all of {{math|SU(2)}} making Schur's lemma applicable.</ref> {{mvar|A}} is a multiple of the identity, which must be {{math|±''I''}} since {{math|1=det ''A'' = 1}}.<ref name=Gelfand_1>{{harvnb|Gelfand|Minlos|Shapiro|1963}} This construction of the covering group is treated in paragraph 4, section 1, chapter 1 in Part II.</ref> The space <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> is mapped to [[Minkowski space]] {{math|'''M'''<sup>4</sup>}}, via
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">X = (\xi_1,\xi_2,\xi_3,\xi_4) \leftrightarrow \overrightarrow{(\xi_1,\xi_2,\xi_3,\xi_4)} = (x,y,z,t) = \overrightarrow{X}.</math>|{{EquationRef|C5|C5}}}}

The action of {{math|'''P'''(''A'')}} on <math>\mathfrak{h}</math> preserves determinants. The induced representation {{math|'''p'''}} of <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> on <math>\R^4,</math> via the above isomorphism, given by
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\mathbf{p}(A)\overrightarrow{X} = \overrightarrow{AXA^\dagger}</math>|{{EquationRef|C6|C6}}}}
preserves the Lorentz inner product since
<math display="block">- \det X = \xi_1^2 + \xi_2^2 +\xi_3^2 -\xi_4^2 = x^2 + y^2 +z^2 - t^2.</math>

This means that {{math|'''p'''(''A'')}} belongs to the full Lorentz group {{math|SO(3; 1)}}. By the [[main theorem of connectedness]], since <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> is connected, its image under {{math|'''p'''}} in {{math|SO(3; 1)}} is connected, and hence is contained in {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}}.

It can be shown that the [[Pushforward (differential)|Lie map]] of <math>\mathbf{p} : \text{SL}(2,\Complex) \to \text{SO}(3; 1)^+,</math> is a Lie algebra isomorphism: <math>\pi : \mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex) \to \mathfrak{so}(3; 1).</math><ref group = nb>Meaning the kernel is trivial, to see this recall that the kernel of a Lie algebra homomorphism is an [[ideal (Lie algebra)|ideal]] and hence a subspace. Since {{math|'''p'''}} is {{math|2:1}} and both <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> and {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} are {{nowrap|{{math|6}}-dimensional}}, the kernel must be {{nowrap|{{math|0}}-dimensional}}, hence {{math|{0}.}}</ref> The map {{math|'''P'''}} is also onto.<ref group=nb>The exponential map is one-to-one in a neighborhood of the identity in <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex),</math> hence the composition <math>\exp \circ \sigma \circ \log : \text{SL}(2,\Complex) \to \text{SO}(3; 1)^+,</math> where {{mvar|σ}} is the Lie algebra isomorphism, is onto an open neighborhood {{math|''U'' ⊂ SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} containing the identity. Such a neighborhood generates the connected component.</ref>

Thus <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math>, since it is simply connected, is the universal covering group of {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}}, isomorphic to the group {{mvar|G}} of above.
{{Hidden end}}

==== Non-surjectiveness of exponential mapping for SL(2, C) ====
[[File:Commutative diagram SO(3, 1) latex.svg|350px|thumb|This diagram shows the web of maps discussed in the text. Here {{mvar|V}} is a finite-dimensional vector space carrying representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex), \mathfrak{so}(3; 1),</math> <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> and <math>\text{SO}(3; 1)^+.</math> <math>\exp</math> is the exponential mapping, {{math|'''p'''}} is the covering map from <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex),</math> onto {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} and {{mvar|σ}} is the Lie algebra isomorphism induced by it.

The maps {{math|Π, ''π''}} and the two {{math|Φ}} are representations. The picture is only partially true when {{math|Π}} is projective.]]

The exponential mapping <math>\exp : \mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex) \to \text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> is not onto.<ref>{{harvnb|Rossmann|2002|loc=Section 2.1.}}</ref> The matrix
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">q = \begin{pmatrix} -1&1\\ 0&-1\\ \end{pmatrix}</math>|{{EquationRef|S6|S6}}}}
is in <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex),</math> but there is no <math>Q\in \mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex)</math> such that {{math|1=''q'' = exp(''Q'')}}.<ref group="nb">{{harvnb|Rossmann|2002}} From Example 4 in section 2.1 : This can be seen as follows. The matrix {{mvar|q}} has eigenvalues {{math|{−1, −1}<nowiki/>}}, but it is not [[Diagonalizable matrix|diagonalizable]]. If {{math|1=''q'' = exp(''Q'')}}, then {{mvar|Q}} has eigenvalues {{math|''λ'', −''λ''}} with {{math|1=''λ'' = ''iπ'' + 2''πik''}} for some {{mvar|k}} because elements of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex)</math> are traceless. But then {{mvar|Q}} is diagonalizable, hence {{mvar|q}} is diagonalizable, which is a contradiction.</ref>

In general, if {{mvar|g}} is an element of a connected Lie group {{mvar|G}} with Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g},</math> then, by {{EquationNote|Lie|(Lie)}},
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">g = \exp(X_1) \cdots \exp(X_n), \qquad X_1, \ldots X_n \in \mathfrak{g}.</math>|{{EquationRef|S7|S7}}}}

The matrix {{mvar|q}} can be written
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\begin{align}
          &\exp(-X)\exp(i\pi H) \\
    {}={} &\exp \left(\begin{pmatrix} 0&-1\\ 0&0\\ \end{pmatrix}\right) \exp \left(i\pi \begin{pmatrix} 1&0\\ 0&-1\\ \end{pmatrix} \right) \\[6pt]
    {}={} &\begin{pmatrix} 1&-1\\ 0&1 \\ \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} -1&0\\ 0&-1\\ \end{pmatrix}\\[6pt]
    {}={} &\begin{pmatrix} -1&1\\ 0&-1\\ \end{pmatrix} \\
    {}={} &q.
\end{align}</math>
 | {{EquationRef|S8|S8}}
}}

=== Realization of representations of {{math|SL(2, C)}} and {{math|sl(2, C)}} and their Lie algebras ===
The complex linear representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex)</math> and <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> are more straightforward to obtain than the <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1)^+</math> representations. The [[Holomorphic function|holomorphic]] group representations (meaning the corresponding Lie algebra representation is complex linear) are related to the complex linear Lie algebra representations by exponentiation. The real linear representations of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex)</math> are exactly the {{math|(''μ'', ''ν'')}}-representations. They can be exponentiated too. The {{math|(''μ'', 0)}}-representations are complex linear and are (isomorphic to) the highest weight-representations. These are usually indexed with only one integer (but half-integers are used here).

The mathematical convention is used in this section for convenience. Lie algebra elements differ by a factor of {{math|''i''}}, and there is no factor of {{math|''i''}} in the exponential mapping compared to the physics convention used elsewhere. Let the basis of  <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex)</math> be{{sfn|Hall|2015|loc=First displayed equations in section 4.6.}}
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">H = \begin{pmatrix} 1&0\\ 0&-1\\ \end{pmatrix}, \quad  X = \begin{pmatrix} 0&1\\ 0&0\\ \end{pmatrix}, \quad Y = \begin{pmatrix} 0&0\\ 1&0\\ \end{pmatrix}.
</math>|{{EquationRef|S1|S1}}}}
This choice of basis and the notation is standard in the mathematical literature.{{sfn|Hall|2015|loc=First displayed equations in section 4.6.}}

==== Complex linear representations ====
The irreducible holomorphic {{math|(''n'' + 1)}}-dimensional representations  <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex), n \geqslant 2,</math> can be realized on the space of [[homogeneous polynomial]] of [[Degree of a polynomial|degree]] {{math|''n''}} in 2 variables <math>\mathbf{P}^2_n,</math><ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015|loc=Example 4.10.}}</ref><ref name="harvnb|Knapp|2001">{{harvnb|Knapp|2001|loc=Chapter 2.}}</ref> the elements of which are

<math display="block">P\begin{pmatrix} z_1\\ z_2\\ \end{pmatrix} = c_n z_1^n + c_{n-1} z_1^{n-1}z_2 + \cdots + c_0 z_2^n, \quad c_0, c_1, \ldots, c_n \in \mathbb Z.</math>

The action of <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> is given by<ref>{{harvnb|Knapp|2001}} Equation 2.1.</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015|loc=Equation 4.2.}}</ref>
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">(\phi_n(g)P)\begin{pmatrix} z_1\\ z_2\\ \end{pmatrix} = \left [\phi_n \begin{pmatrix} a&b\\ c&d\\ \end{pmatrix} P\right ] \begin{pmatrix} z_1\\ z_2\\ \end{pmatrix} =
P\left( \begin{pmatrix} a&b\\ c&d\\ \end{pmatrix}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} z_1\\ z_2\\ \end{pmatrix} \right ), \qquad P \in \mathbf{P}^2_n.</math>|{{EquationRef|S2|S2}}}}

The associated <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex)</math>-action is, using {{EquationNote|G6|(G6)}} and the definition above, for the basis elements of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex),</math><ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015|loc=Equation before 4.5.}}</ref>
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\phi_n(H) = -z_1\frac{\partial}{\partial z_1} + z_2\frac{\partial}{\partial z_2}, \quad \phi_n(X) = -z_2\frac{\partial}{\partial z_1}, \quad \phi_n(Y) = -z_1\frac{\partial}{\partial z_2}.</math>|{{EquationRef|S5|S5}}}}

With a choice of basis for <math>P \in \mathbf{P}^2_{n}</math>, these representations become matrix Lie algebras.

==== Real linear representations ====
The {{math|(''μ'', ''ν'')}}-representations are realized on a space of polynomials <math>\mathbf{P}^2_{\mu,\nu}</math> in <math>z_1, \overline{z_1}, z_2, \overline{z_2},</math> homogeneous of degree {{mvar|μ}} in <math>z_1, z_2</math> and homogeneous of degree {{mvar|ν}} in <math>\overline{z_1}, \overline{z_2}.</math><ref name="harvnb|Knapp|2001"/> The representations are given by<ref>{{harvnb|Knapp|2001}} Equation 2.4.</ref>
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">(\phi_{\mu,\nu}(g)P)\begin{pmatrix} z_1\\ z_2\\ \end{pmatrix} =\left [\phi_{\mu,\nu} \begin{pmatrix} a&b\\ c&d\\ \end{pmatrix} P\right ] \begin{pmatrix} z_1\\ z_2\\ \end{pmatrix} =
P \left( \begin{pmatrix} a&b\\ c&d\\ \end{pmatrix}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} z_1\\ z_2\\ \end{pmatrix} \right ), \quad P \in \mathbf{P}^2_{\mu,\nu}.</math>|{{EquationRef|S6|S6}}}}

By employing {{EquationNote|G6|(G6)}} again it is found that
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\begin{align}
\phi_{\mu,\nu}(E)P =  &- \frac{\partial P}{\partial z_1} \left (E_{11}z_1 + E_{12}z_2 \right ) - \frac{\partial P}{\partial z_2} \left (E_{21}z_1 + E_{22}z_2 \right) \\
&- \frac{\partial P}{\partial \overline{z_1}}\left (\overline{E_{11}}\overline{z_1} + \overline{E_{12}}\overline{z_2} \right ) -\frac{\partial P}{\partial \overline{z_2}} \left (\overline{E_{21}}\overline{z_1} + \overline{E_{22}}\overline{z_2} \right )
\end{align}, \quad E \in \mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbf{C}).</math>|{{EquationRef|S7|S7}}}}

In particular for the basis elements,
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\begin{align}
\phi_{\mu,\nu}(H) &= -z_1\frac{\partial}{\partial z_1} + z_2\frac{\partial}{\partial z_2}-\overline{z_1}\frac{\partial}{\partial \overline{z_1}} + \overline{z_2}\frac{\partial}{\partial \overline{z_2}} \\
\phi_{\mu,\nu}(X) &= -z_2\frac{\partial}{\partial z_1} - \overline{z_2}\frac{\partial}{\partial \overline{z_1}} \\
\phi_{\mu,\nu}(Y) &= -z_1\frac{\partial}{\partial z_2} - \overline{z_1}\frac{\partial}{\partial \overline{z_2}}
\end{align}</math>|{{EquationRef|S8|S8}}}}

=== Properties of the (''m'', ''n'') representations ===
The {{math|(''m'', ''n'')}} representations, defined above via {{EquationNote|A1|(A1)}} (as restrictions to the real form <math>\mathfrak{sl}(3, 1)</math>) of tensor products of irreducible complex linear representations {{math|1=''π''<sub>''m'' = ''μ''</sub>}} and {{math|1=''π''<sub>''n'' = ''ν''</sub>}} of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex),</math> are irreducible, and they are the only irreducible representations.<ref name="ReferenceC" />
*Irreducibility follows from the unitarian trick<ref name="Knapp 2001">{{harvnb|Knapp|2001|loc=Section 2.3.}}</ref> and that a representation {{math|Π}} of {{math|SU(2) × SU(2)}} is irreducible if and only if {{math|1=Π = Π<sub>μ</sub> ⊗ Π<sub>ν</sub>}},<ref group=nb>{{harvnb|Rossmann|2002|loc=Proposition 10, paragraph 6.3.}} This is easiest proved using [[character theory]].</ref> where {{math|Π<sub>μ</sub>, Π<sub>ν</sub>}} are irreducible representations of {{math|SU(2)}}.
*Uniqueness follows from that the {{math|Π<sub>''m''</sub>}} are the only irreducible representations of {{math|SU(2)}}, which is one of the conclusions of the theorem of the highest weight.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015|loc=Theorems 9.4–5.}}</ref>

==== Casimir operators ====
For the Lorentz Lie algebra, the [[Casimir operator]]s are central elements of the [[universal enveloping algebra]], hence by [[Schur's lemma]] they act by scalars on each irreducible representation.<ref>{{harvnb|Bekaert|Boulanger|2006|p=3}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}}</ref> For the finite-dimensional theory it is convenient to pass to the complexification and use the decomposition
<math display="block">
\mathfrak{so}(3,1)_\mathbb C \cong \mathbf A_{\mathbb C} \oplus \mathbf B_{\mathbb C},
</math>
where each of <math>\mathbf A_{\mathbb C}</math> and <math>\mathbf B_{\mathbb C}</math> is a copy of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb C)</math> (treated here as <math>\mathfrak{su}(2)_{\mathbb C}</math>, as [[#Lie algebra|above]], with the generators <math>A_i</math> and <math>B_i</math>, respectively).<ref name="weinberg-2002-5.6">{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Section 5.6}}</ref>

With this normalization, quadratic Casimirs for the two factors may be taken as
<math display="block">
\Omega_A=A_1^2+A_2^2+A_3^2,\qquad
\Omega_B=B_1^2+B_2^2+B_3^2.
</math>
Equivalently, if <math>A_\pm=A_1\pm iA_2</math> and <math>B_\pm=B_1\pm iB_2</math>, then
<math display="block">
\Omega_A=A_3^2+\frac12(A_+A_-+A_-A_+),\qquad
\Omega_B=B_3^2+\frac12(B_+B_-+B_-B_+).
</math>
Since the two factors commute, <math>\Omega_A</math> and <math>\Omega_B</math> are central in the universal enveloping algebra of <math>\mathfrak{so}(3,1)_\mathbb C</math>. A convenient normalized choice of algebraically independent quadratic Casimir operators for the Lorentz algebra is therefore
<math display="block">
C_1=2(\Omega_A+\Omega_B),\qquad
C_2=\Omega_A-\Omega_B.
</math>

In terms of the rotation and boost generators, this becomes
<math display="block">
C_1=\mathbf J^2-\mathbf K^2,\qquad
C_2=i\,\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf K.
</math>
If {{math|(m,n)}} denotes the irreducible representation obtained from the spin-{{mvar|m}} representation of <math>\mathfrak a</math> and the spin-{{mvar|n}} representation of <math>\mathfrak b</math>, then
<math display="block">
\Omega_A\mapsto m(m+1),\qquad
\Omega_B\mapsto n(n+1),
</math>
and hence
<math display="block">
C_1\mapsto 2\bigl(m(m+1)+n(n+1)\bigr),\qquad
C_2\mapsto m(m+1)-n(n+1).
</math>
In particular, the conjugate pair {{math|(m,n)}} and {{math|(n,m)}} have the same value of <math>C_1</math> but opposite values of <math>C_2</math>; when {{math|1=m=n}}, the second Casimir vanishes.<ref name="weinberg-2002-5.6" />

==== Dimension ====
The {{math|(''m'', ''n'')}} representations are {{math|(2''m'' + 1)(2''n'' + 1)}}-dimensional.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Chapter 5.}}</ref> This follows easiest from counting the dimensions in any concrete realization, such as the one given in [[#representations of SL(2, C) and sl(2, C)|representations of <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> and <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2, \Complex)</math>]]. For a Lie general algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> the [[Weyl character formula#Weyl dimension formula|Weyl dimension formula]],<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015|loc= Theorem 10.18.}}</ref>
<math display="block">\dim\pi_\rho = \frac{\Pi_{\alpha \in R^+} \langle\alpha, \rho + \delta \rangle}{\Pi_{\alpha \in R^+} \langle\alpha, \delta \rangle},</math>
applies, where {{math|''R''<sup>+</sup>}} is the set of positive roots, {{math|''ρ''}} is the highest weight, and {{math|''δ''}} is half the sum of the positive roots. The inner product <math>\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle</math> is that of the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g},</math> invariant under the action of the Weyl group on <math>\mathfrak{h} \subset \mathfrak{g},</math> the [[Cartan subalgebra]]. The roots (really elements of <math>\mathfrak{h}^*</math>) are via this inner product identified with elements of <math>\mathfrak{h}.</math> For <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex),</math> the formula reduces to {{math|1=dim ''π<sub>μ</sub>'' = 2''μ'' + 1 = 2''m'' + 1}}, ''where the present notation must be taken into account''. The highest weight is {{math|2''μ''}}.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2003|p=235.}}</ref> By taking tensor products, the result follows.

==== Faithfulness ====
If a (nontrivial) representation {{math|Π}} of a Lie group {{math|''G''}} is not faithful, then {{math|1=''N'' = ker Π}} is a nontrivial normal subgroup.<ref>See any text on basic group theory.</ref> There are three relevant cases.
#{{math|''N''}} is non-discrete and [[abelian group|abelian]].
#{{math|''N''}} is non-discrete and non-abelian.
#{{math|''N''}} is discrete. In this case {{math|''N'' ⊂ ''Z''}}, where {{math|''Z''}} is the center of {{math|''G''}}.<ref group=nb>Any discrete normal subgroup of a [[path connected]] group {{math|''G''}} is contained in the center {{math|''Z''}} of {{math|''G''}}.
{{Paragraph break}}
{{harvnb|Hall|2015|loc=Exercise 11, chapter 1.}}</ref>
In the case of {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}}, the first case is excluded since {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} is semi-simple.<ref group=nb>A semisimple Lie group does not have any non-discrete normal [[abelian group|abelian subgroups]]. This can be taken as the definition of semisimplicity.</ref> The second case (and the first case) is excluded because {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} is simple.<ref group=nb>A simple group does not have any non-discrete normal subgroups.</ref> For the third case, {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} is isomorphic to the quotient <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)/\{\pm I\}.</math> But <math>\{\pm I\}</math> is the center of <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex).</math> It follows that the center of {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} is trivial, and this excludes the third case. The conclusion is that every representation {{math|Π : SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup> → GL(''V'')}} and every projective representation {{math|Π : SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup> → PGL(''W'')}} for {{math|''V'', ''W''}} finite-dimensional vector spaces are faithful.

By using the fundamental Lie correspondence, the statements and the reasoning above translate directly to Lie algebras with (abelian) nontrivial non-discrete normal subgroups replaced by (one-dimensional) nontrivial ideals in the Lie algebra,<ref>{{harvnb|Rossmann|2002}} Propositions 3 and 6 paragraph 2.5.</ref> and the center of {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} replaced by the center of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(3; 1)^+</math>The center of any semisimple Lie algebra is trivial<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2003}} See exercise 1, Chapter 6.</ref> and <math>\mathfrak{so}(3; 1)</math> is semi-simple and simple, and hence has no non-trivial ideals.

A related fact is that if the corresponding representation of <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> is faithful, then the representation is projective. Conversely, if the representation is non-projective, then the corresponding <math>\text{SL}(2,\Complex)</math> representation is not faithful, but is {{math|2:1}}.

==== Non-unitarity ====
The {{math|(''m'', ''n'')}} Lie algebra representation is not [[Hermitian]]. Accordingly, the corresponding (projective) representation of the group is never [[unitary matrix|unitary]].<ref group=nb>By contrast, there is a trick, also called Weyl's unitarian trick, but unrelated to the unitarian trick of above showing that all finite-dimensional representations are, or can be made, unitary. If {{math|(Π, ''V'')}} is a finite-dimensional representation of a ''compact'' Lie group {{mvar|G}} and if {{math|(·, ·)}} is any [[inner product]] on {{mvar|V}}, define a new inner product {{math|(·, ·)<sub>Π</sub>}} by {{math|1=(''x'', ''y'')<sub>Π</sub> = ∫<sub>''G''</sub>(Π(''g'')''x'', Π(''g'')''y'') ''dμ''(''g'')}}, where {{mvar|μ}} is [[Haar measure]] on {{mvar|G}}. Then {{math|Π}} is unitary with respect to {{math|(·, ·)<sub>Π</sub>}}. See {{harvtxt|Hall|2015|loc=Theorem 4.28.}}
{{Paragraph break}}
Another consequence is that every compact Lie group has the ''complete reducibility property'', meaning that all its finite-dimensional representations decompose as a direct sum of ''irreducible'' representations. {{harvtxt|Hall|2015|loc=Definition 4.24., Theorem 4.28.}}
{{Paragraph break}}
It is also true that there are no infinite-dimensional ''irreducible'' unitary representations of compact Lie groups, stated, but not proved in {{harvtxt|Greiner|Müller|1994|loc=Section 15.2.}}.</ref> This is due to the non-compactness of the Lorentz group. In fact, a connected simple non-compact Lie group cannot have ''any'' nontrivial unitary finite-dimensional representations.<ref name="Wigner 1939"/> There is a topological proof of this.<ref>{{harvnb|Bekaert|Boulanger|2006}} p.4.</ref> Let {{math|''u'' : ''G'' → GL(''V'')}}, where {{math|''V''}} is finite-dimensional, be a continuous unitary representation of the non-compact connected simple Lie group {{mvar|G}}. Then {{math|''u''(''G'') ⊂ U(''V'') ⊂ GL(''V'')}} where {{math|U(''V'')}} is the compact subgroup of {{math|GL(''V'')}} consisting of unitary transformations of {{mvar|V}}. The [[Kernel (algebra)|kernel]] of {{math|''u''}} is a [[normal subgroup]] of {{mvar|G}}. Since {{mvar|G}} is simple, {{math|ker ''u''}} is either all of {{mvar|G}}, in which case {{math|''u''}} is trivial, or {{math|ker ''u''}} is trivial, in which case {{math|''u''}} is [[Faithful representation|faithful]]. In the latter case {{math|''u''}} is a [[diffeomorphism]] onto its image,<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2003}} Proposition 1.20.</ref> {{math|''u''(''G'') ≅ ''G''}} and {{math|''u''(''G'')}} is a Lie group. This would mean that {{math|''u''(''G'')}} is an [[Embedded submanifold|embedded]] non-compact Lie subgroup of the compact group {{math|U(''V'')}}. This is impossible with the subspace topology on {{math|''u''(''G'') ⊂ U(''V'')}} since all ''embedded'' Lie subgroups of a Lie group are closed<ref>{{harvnb|Lee|2003|loc=Theorem 8.30.}}</ref> If {{math|''u''(''G'')}} were closed, it would be compact,<ref group=nb>{{harvnb|Lee|2003}} Lemma A.17 (c). Closed subsets of compact sets are compact.</ref> and then {{mvar|G}} would be compact,<ref group=nb>{{harvnb|Lee|2003}} Lemma A.17 (a). If {{math|''f'' : ''X'' → ''Y''}} is continuous, {{mvar|X}} is compact, then {{math|''f''(''X'')}} is compact.</ref> contrary to assumption.<ref group=nb>The non-unitarity is a vital ingredient in the proof of the [[Coleman–Mandula theorem]], which has the implication that, contrary to in non-relativistic theories, there can exist no ''ordinary'' symmetry relating particles of different spin. See {{harvtxt|Weinberg|2000|loch=Chapter 24.}}</ref>

In the case of the Lorentz group, this can also be seen directly from the definitions. The representations of {{math|'''A'''}} and {{math|'''B'''}} used in the construction are Hermitian. This means that {{math|'''J'''}} is Hermitian, but {{math|'''K'''}} is [[anti-Hermitian]].<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Section 5.6, p. 231.}}</ref> The non-unitarity is not a problem in quantum field theory, since the objects of concern are not required to have a Lorentz-invariant positive definite norm.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Section 5.6.}}</ref>

==== Restriction to SO(3) ====
The {{math|(''m'', ''n'')}} representation is, however, unitary when restricted to the rotation subgroup {{math|SO(3)}}, but these representations are not irreducible as representations of SO(3). A [[Clebsch–Gordan coefficients|Clebsch–Gordan decomposition]] can be applied showing that an {{math|(''m'', ''n'')}} representation have {{math|SO(3)}}-invariant subspaces of highest weight (spin) {{math|''m'' + ''n'', ''m'' + ''n'' − 1, ..., {{abs| ''m'' − ''n''}}}},<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|p=231.}}</ref> where each possible highest weight (spin) occurs exactly once. A weight subspace of highest weight (spin) {{math|''j''}} is {{math|(2''j'' + 1)}}-dimensional. So for example, the ({{sfrac|1|2}}, {{sfrac|1|2}}) representation has spin&nbsp;1 and spin&nbsp;0 subspaces of dimension 3 and 1 respectively.

Since the [[angular momentum]] operator is given by {{math|1='''J''' = '''A''' + '''B'''}}, the highest spin in quantum mechanics of the rotation sub-representation will be {{math|(''m'' + ''n'')ℏ}} and the "usual" rules of addition of angular momenta and the formalism of [[3-j symbol]]s, [[6-j symbol]]s, etc. applies.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Sections 2.5, 5.7.}}</ref>

==== Spinors ====
It is the {{math|SO(3)}}-invariant subspaces of the irreducible representations that determine whether a representation has spin. From the above paragraph, it is seen that the {{math|(''m'', ''n'')}} representation has spin if {{math|''m'' + ''n''}} is half-integer. The simplest are {{math|({{sfrac|1|2}}, 0)}} and {{math|(0, {{sfrac|1|2}})}}, the Weyl-spinors of dimension {{math|2}}. Then, for example, {{math|(0, {{sfrac|3|2}})}} and {{math|(1, {{sfrac|1|2}})}} are a spin representations of dimensions {{math|1=2⋅{{sfrac|3|2}} + 1 = 4}} and {{math|1=(2 + 1)(2⋅{{sfrac|1|2}} + 1) = 6}} respectively. According to the above paragraph, there are subspaces with spin both {{math|{{sfrac|3|2}}}} and {{math|{{sfrac|1|2}}}} in the last two cases, so these representations cannot likely represent a ''single'' physical particle which must be well-behaved under {{math|SO(3)}}. It cannot be ruled out in general, however, that representations with multiple {{math|SO(3)}} subrepresentations with different spin can represent physical particles with well-defined spin. It may be that there is a suitable relativistic wave equation that projects out ''unphysical components'', leaving only a single spin.<ref>{{harvnb|Tung|1985|loc=Section 10.5.}}</ref>

Construction of pure spin {{math|{{sfrac|''n''|2}}}} representations for any {{math|''n''}} (under {{math|SO(3)}}) from the irreducible representations involves taking tensor products of the Dirac-representation with a non-spin representation, extraction of a suitable subspace, and finally imposing differential constraints.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002}} This is outlined (very briefly) on page 232, hardly more than a footnote.</ref>

==== Dual representations ====
[[File:Root system A1xA1.svg|200px|thumb|right| The [[root system]] {{math|''A''<sub>1</sub> × ''A''<sub>1</sub>}} of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex) \oplus \mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex).</math>]]

The following theorems are applied to examine whether the [[dual representation]] of an irreducible representation is [[Representation theory#Equivariant maps and isomorphisms|isomorphic]] to the original representation:
#The set of [[Weight (representation theory)|weights]] of the [[dual representation]] of an irreducible representation of a semisimple Lie algebra is, including multiplicities, the negative of the set of weights for the original representation.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2003|loc=Proposition 7.39.}}</ref>
#Two irreducible representations are isomorphic if and only if they have the same [[highest weight]].<ref group=nb>This is one of the conclusions of [[Theorem on highest weights|Cartan's theorem]], the theorem of the highest weight.{{Paragraph break}}{{harvtxt|Hall|2015|loc=Theorems 9.4–5.}}</ref>
#For each semisimple Lie algebra there exists a unique element {{math|w<sub>0</sub>}} of the [[Weyl group]] such that if {{math|''μ''}} is a dominant integral weight, then {{math|''w''<sub>0</sub> ⋅ (−''μ'')}} is again a dominant integral weight.<ref name="Hall 2003 loc=Theorem 7.40">{{harvnb|Hall|2003|loc=Theorem 7.40.}}</ref>
#If <math>\pi_{\mu_0}</math> is an irreducible representation with highest weight {{math|''μ''<sub>0</sub>}}, then <math>\pi^*_{\mu_0}</math> has highest weight {{math|''w''<sub>0</sub> ⋅ (−''μ'')}}.<ref name="Hall 2003 loc=Theorem 7.40"/>
Here, the elements of the Weyl group are considered as orthogonal transformations, acting by matrix multiplication, on the real vector space of [[root system|roots]]. If {{math|−''I''}} is an element of the [[Weyl group]] of a semisimple Lie algebra, then {{math|1=''w''<sub>0</sub> = −''I''}}. In the case of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex),</math> the Weyl group is {{math|1=''W'' = {''I'', −''I''}<nowiki/>}}.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2003|loc=Section 6.6.}}</ref> It follows that each {{math|1=''π<sub>μ</sub>'', ''μ'' = 0, 1, ...}} is isomorphic to its dual <math>\pi^*_{\mu}.</math> The root system of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex) \oplus \mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex)</math> is shown in the figure to the right.<ref group=nb>{{harvnb|Hall|2015|loc=Section 8.2}} The root system is the union of two copies of {{math|''A''<sub>1</sub>}}, where each copy resides in its own dimensions in the embedding vector space.</ref> The Weyl group is generated by <math>\{w_{\gamma}\}</math> where <math>w_\gamma</math> is reflection in the plane orthogonal to {{math|''γ''}} as {{math|''γ''}} ranges over all roots.<ref group=nb>{{harvnb|Rossmann|2002}} This definition is equivalent to the definition in terms of the connected Lie group whose Lie algebra is the Lie algebra of the root system under consideration.</ref> Inspection shows that {{math|1=''w''<sub>''α''</sub> ⋅ ''w''<sub>''β''</sub> = −''I''}} so {{math|−''I'' ∈ ''W''}}. Using the fact that if {{math|''π'', ''σ''}} are Lie algebra representations and {{math|''π'' ≅ ''σ''}}, then {{math|Π ≅ Σ}},<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2003|loc=Second item in proposition 4.5.}}</ref> the conclusion for {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} is
<math display="block">\pi_{m, n}^{*} \cong \pi_{m, n}, \quad \Pi_{m, n}^{*} \cong \Pi_{m, n}, \quad 2m, 2n \in \mathbf{N}. </math>

==== Complex conjugate representations ====
If {{math|π}} is a representation of a Lie algebra, then <math>\overline{\pi}</math> is a representation, where the bar denotes entry-wise complex conjugation in the representative matrices. This follows from that complex conjugation commutes with addition and multiplication.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2003|p=219.}}</ref> In general, every irreducible representation {{math|π}} of <math>\mathfrak{sl}(n,\Complex)</math> can be written uniquely as {{math|1=π = π<sup>+</sup> + π<sup>−</sup>}}, where<ref>{{harvnb|Rossmann|2002|loc=Exercise 3 in paragraph 6.5.}}</ref>
<math display="block">\pi^\pm(X) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\pi(X) \pm i\pi\left(i^{-1}X\right)\right),</math>
with <math>\pi^+</math> holomorphic (complex linear) and <math>\pi^-</math> '''anti-holomorphic''' (conjugate linear). For <math>\mathfrak{sl}(2,\Complex),</math> since <math>\pi_\mu</math> is holomorphic, <math>\overline{\pi_\mu}</math> is anti-holomorphic. Direct examination of the explicit expressions for <math>\pi_{\mu, 0}</math> and <math>\pi_{0, \nu}</math> in equation {{EquationNote|S8|(S8)}} below shows that they are holomorphic and anti-holomorphic respectively. Closer examination of the expression {{EquationNote|S8|(S8)}} also allows for identification of <math>\pi^+</math> and <math>\pi^-</math> for <math>\pi_{\mu, \nu}</math> as
<math display="block">\pi^+_{\mu, \nu} = \pi_\mu^{\oplus_{\nu+1}},\qquad \pi^-_{\mu, \nu} = \overline{\pi_\nu^{\oplus_{\mu+1}}}.</math>

Using the above identities (interpreted as pointwise addition of functions), for {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}} yields
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \overline{\pi_{m, n}} &= \overline{\pi_{m, n}^+ + \pi_{m, n}^-}=\overline{\pi_m^{\oplus_{2n + 1}}} + \overline{\overline{\pi_n}^{\oplus_{2m + 1}}} \\

 &=\pi_n^{\oplus_{2m + 1}} + \overline{\pi_m}^{\oplus_{2n + 1}} =
    \pi_{n, m}^+ + \pi_{n, m}^- = \pi_{n, m} \\
                        & &&2m, 2n \in \mathbb{N} \\
  \overline{\Pi_{m, n}} &= \Pi_{n, m}
\end{align}</math>
where the statement for the group representations follow from {{math|1=exp({{overline|''X''}}) = {{overline|exp(''X'')}}}}. It follows that the irreducible representations {{math|(''m'', ''n'')}} have real matrix representatives if and only if {{math|1=''m'' = ''n''}}. Reducible representations on the form {{math|(''m'', ''n'') ⊕ (''n'', ''m'')}} have real matrices too.

=== Adjoint representation, Clifford algebra, and Dirac spinor representation ===
[[File:Richard Brauer.jpg|upright|thumb|right|[[Richard Brauer]] and wife Ilse 1970. Brauer generalized the [[spin representation]]s of Lie algebras sitting inside [[Clifford algebra]]s to spin higher than {{sfrac|1|2}}. {{Paragraph break}}Photo courtesy of MFO.]]

In general representation theory, if {{math|(''π'', ''V'')}} is a representation of a Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g},</math> then there is an associated representation of <math>\mathfrak{g},</math> on {{math|[[Endomorphism|End]](''V'')}}, also denoted {{mvar|π}}, given by
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\pi(X)(A) = [\pi(X), A],\qquad A \in \operatorname{End}(V),\ X \in \mathfrak{g}.</math>|{{EquationRef|I1|I1}}}}

Likewise, a representation {{math|(Π, ''V'')}} of a group {{mvar|G}} yields a representation {{math|Π}} on {{math|End(''V'')}} of {{mvar|G}}, still denoted {{math|Π}}, given by<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2003}} See appendix D.3</ref>
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\Pi(g)(A) = \Pi(g)A\Pi(g)^{-1},\qquad A \in \operatorname{End}(V),\ g \in G.</math>|{{EquationRef|I2|I2}}}}

If {{mvar|π}} and {{math|Π}} are the standard representations on <math>\R^4</math> and if the action is restricted to <math>\mathfrak{so}(3, 1) \subset \text{End}(\R^4),</math>  then the two above representations are the [[adjoint representation of a Lie algebra|adjoint representation of the Lie algebra]] and the [[adjoint representation|adjoint representation of the group]] respectively. The corresponding representations (some <math>\R^n</math> or <math>\Complex^n</math>) always exist for any matrix Lie group, and are paramount for investigation of the representation theory in general, and for any given Lie group in particular.

Applying this to the Lorentz group, if {{math|(Π, ''V'')}} is a projective representation, then direct calculation using {{EquationNote|G5|(G5)}} shows that the induced representation on {{math|End(''V'')}} is a proper representation, i.e. a representation without phase factors.

In quantum mechanics this means that if {{math|(''π'', ''H'')}} or {{math|(Π, ''H'')}} is a representation acting on some Hilbert space {{mvar|H}}, then the corresponding induced representation acts on the set of linear operators on {{mvar|H}}. As an example, the induced representation of the projective spin {{math|({{sfrac|1|2}}, 0) ⊕ (0, {{sfrac|1|2}})}} representation on {{math|End(''H'')}} is the non-projective 4-vector ({{sfrac|1|2}}, {{sfrac|1|2}}) representation.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Equation 5.4.8.}}</ref>

For simplicity, consider only the "discrete part" of {{math|End(''H'')}}, that is, given a basis for {{mvar|H}}, the set of constant matrices of various dimension, including possibly infinite dimensions. The induced 4-vector representation of above on this simplified {{math|End(''H'')}} has an invariant 4-dimensional subspace that is spanned by the four [[gamma matrices]].<ref name="Weinberg 2002 loc=Section 5.4">{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Section 5.4.}}</ref> (The metric convention is different in the linked article.) In a corresponding way, the complete Clifford [[spacetime algebra|algebra of spacetime]], <math>\mathcal{Cl}_{3,1}(\R),</math> whose complexification is <math>\text{M}(4, \Complex),</math> generated by the gamma matrices decomposes as a direct sum of [[representation space]]s of a '''scalar''' irreducible representation (irrep), the {{math|(0, 0)}}, a '''pseudoscalar''' irrep, also the {{math|(0, 0)}}, but with parity inversion eigenvalue {{math|−1}}, see the [[#Space inversion and time reversal|next section]] below, the already mentioned '''vector''' irrep, {{math|({{sfrac|1|2}}, {{sfrac|1|2}})}}, a '''pseudovector''' irrep, {{math|({{sfrac|1|2}}, {{sfrac|1|2}})}} with parity inversion eigenvalue +1 (not −1), and a '''tensor''' irrep, {{math|(1, 0) ⊕ (0, 1)}}.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|pp=215–216.}}</ref> The dimensions add up to {{math|1=1 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 6 = 16}}. In other words,
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\mathcal{Cl}_{3,1}(\R) = (0,0) \oplus \left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right) \oplus [(1, 0) \oplus (0, 1)] \oplus \left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)_p \oplus (0, 0)_p,</math>|{{EquationRef|I3|I3}}}}
where, as is [[Abuse of notation|customary]], a representation is confused with its representation space.

==== {{math|({{sfrac|1|2}}, 0) ⊕ (0, {{sfrac|1|2}})}} spin representation ====

The six-dimensional representation space of the tensor {{math|(1, 0) ⊕ (0, 1)}}-representation inside <math>\mathcal{Cl}_{3,1}(\R)</math> has two roles. The<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002|loc=Equation 5.4.6.}}</ref>
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\sigma^{\mu\nu} = -\frac{i}{4} \left[\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu\right],</math>|{{EquationRef|I4|I4}}}}
where <math>\gamma^0, \ldots, \gamma^3 \in \mathcal{Cl}_{3,1}(\R)</math> are the gamma matrices, the sigmas, only {{math|6}} of which are non-zero due to antisymmetry of the bracket, span the tensor representation space. Moreover, they have the commutation relations of the Lorentz Lie algebra,<ref name="ReferenceA">{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002}} Section 5.4.</ref>
{{NumBlk||<math display="block">\left[\sigma^{\mu\nu}, \sigma^{\rho\tau}\right] = i \left(\eta^{\tau\mu}\sigma^{\rho\nu} + \eta^{\nu\tau}\sigma^{\mu\rho} - \eta^{\rho\mu}\sigma^{\tau\nu} - \eta^{\nu\rho}\sigma^{\mu\tau}\right),</math>|{{EquationRef|I5|I5}}}}
and hence constitute a representation (in addition to spanning a representation space) sitting inside <math>\mathcal{Cl}_{3,1}(\R),</math> the {{math|({{sfrac|1|2}}, 0) ⊕ (0, {{sfrac|1|2}})}} spin representation. For details, see [[Dirac spinor]] and [[Dirac algebra]].

The conclusion is that every element of the complexified <math>\mathcal{Cl}_{3,1}(\R)</math> in {{math|End(''H'')}} (i.e. every complex {{gaps|4|×|4}} matrix) has well defined Lorentz transformation properties. In addition, it has a spin-representation of the Lorentz Lie algebra, which upon exponentiation becomes a spin representation of the group, acting on <math>\Complex^4,</math> making it a space of Dirac spinors.

=== Reducible representations ===
Other representations can be deduced from the irreducible ones, such as those obtained by taking direct sums, tensor products, and quotients of the irreducible representations. Other methods of obtaining representations include the restriction of a representation of a larger group containing the Lorentz group, e.g. <math>\text{GL}(n,\R)</math> and the Poincaré group. These representations are in general not irreducible.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015|loc=Section 4.4}}</ref>

The Lorentz group and its Lie algebra have the ''complete reducibility property''. This means that every representation reduces to a direct sum of irreducible representations.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015|loc=Section 4.4.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|van der Waerden|1974|p=119}}</ref>

=== Space inversion and time reversal ===

The (possibly projective) {{math|(''m'', ''n'')}} representation is irreducible as a representation {{math|SO(3; 1)<sup>+</sup>}}, the identity component of the Lorentz group, in physics terminology the [[orthochronous|proper orthochronous]] Lorentz group. If {{math|1=''m'' = ''n''}} it can be extended to a representation of all of {{math|O(3; 1)}}, the full Lorentz group, including [[P-symmetry|space parity inversion]] and [[T-symmetry|time reversal]]. The representations {{math|(''m'', ''n'') ⊕ (''n'', ''m'')}} can be extended likewise.<ref>{{harvnb|Weinberg|2002| loc=Section 5.7, pp. 232–233.}}</ref>

====Space parity inversion====
